working_title: Electric or Push Trolley: How to Actually Choose the Right One for UK Golf
angle: Most buying guides focus on product rankings; this post instead works through the practical decision-making process — course terrain, boot space, budget, and how often you play — to help a regular UK walker figure out which trolley type genuinely suits them, rather than defaulting to 'electric is always better'.
research_notes:
- Push trolleys are significantly cheaper than electric models and are generally lighter and easier to store; most fold flat or into a compact footprint suited to smaller car boots
- Electric trolleys are heavier due to motor and battery hardware, though weight is mainly a transport concern rather than an on-course one since you're not pushing the load
- Push trolleys typically include more onboard storage as standard (phone pocket, ball holder, umbrella slot, drink holder); many electric models require paid accessory add-ons for equivalent storage
- Electric options offer meaningful advantages on hilly/undulating UK courses: powered traction, consistent speed, and downhill braking/control
- Three main electric sub-types exist: manual-steer electric (most common), remote-control, and follow (autonomous) — follow models are the most expensive category
- Key electric features worth paying for on UK courses: downhill/slope braking control (DHC on Motocaddy, EBS on PowaKaddy), lithium battery (lighter, better range than older lead-acid), reliable one-step fold
- GPS built into trolley is a nice-to-have but adds cost; golfers who already own a separate GPS device or use a phone may not need it
- Rough price tiers for electric UK market (2026): entry-level lithium ~£300–£450, mid-range with GPS ~£450–£650, premium remote/follow models above that
- Push trolleys: well-regarded UK-market models include Motocaddy Cube Push, PowaKaddy Micra, Clicgear 4.0, Stewart R1-S (UK-made), PowaKaddy DLX-Lite FF
- Electric models frequently mentioned in UK 2026 guides: Motocaddy SE / SE Ultra (entry), Motocaddy M5 GPS DHC (mid), PowaKaddy CT6 (compact fold), Motocaddy M7 GPS Remote (premium), Stewart Golf Q Follow (top-end)
- Two-wheel pull trolleys still exist as a basic/cheap option but three-wheel push is generally easier on the body as you push weight ahead rather than twist arm pulling behind
- Lithium batteries on quality electric trolleys typically deliver 18–36 holes per charge depending on model and terrain; forgetting to charge is a genuine and commonly cited practical downside
- UK-specific terrain consideration: many UK links and heathland courses are undulating enough that downhill braking is a meaningful safety/practicality feature, not just a gimmick
- Boot/storage space is a real practical factor for UK golfers; electric trolleys fold down but remain bulkier and heavier than push equivalents
